title: Fossils & Evolution
intro: Fossils are the preserved evidence of past life. Learn HOW they form (and why so few do), how they date rocks (index fossils), and how evolution, natural selection and extinction explain the changing fossil record.

sections.title: Fossils, fossil ranges and index fossils

boxes.text: Why does fossil succession work? Species appear (evolve) and disappear (go extinct) and do not come back. So each slice of Earth history has its own mix of species. Where two ranges overlap, the overlap is an even narrower slice of time. Think of a pile of old magazines: each issue was printed in one year, so the issues in a pile tell you roughly the year.
FAD = First Appearance Datum. LAD = Last Appearance Datum. In a rock column the oldest layer is at the bottom, so a species' FAD sits lower than its LAD.

Do not mix up a fossil range with an index fossil. A species that lived a very long time is a poor index fossil. A short-ranging, widespread one is the good one. The textbook says the average species lifespan in the fossil record is about a million years.

images.alt: Text naming the first appearance datum (FAD) and the last appearance datum (LAD).
Photo of a fossil fish skeleton pressed into pale rock.
Photo of an open museum drawer holding fossil fish slabs, spiral ammonite shells and a large jaw bone.

img.alt: Text naming the first appearance datum (FAD) and the last appearance datum (LAD).

steps.title: First and last appearance
bullets: The **fossil range** is the span from a species' first appearance to its last appearance. Each fossil species has its own unique range, and ranges can overlap.
**FAD** = first appearance datum. **LAD** = last appearance datum.
**Index fossils** are diagnostic of one geologic time, so finding one tells you roughly how old the layer is. The best ones were geographically widespread and lived only a **narrow time interval**.

img.alt: Photo of a fossil fish skeleton pressed into pale rock.

steps.title: A fossil fish in rock
bullets: **Fossils** are any evidence of past life preserved in rock: real body parts (rare), impressions, casts and molds, parts replaced by minerals, or signs of behaviour such as footprints and burrows.
This fish skeleton is a typical example: the animal is long dead, but its shape is kept in the rock.

img.alt: Photo of an open museum drawer holding fossil fish slabs, spiral ammonite shells and a large jaw bone.

steps.title: Fossils collected and stored
bullets: A museum drawer holds fossil fish, ammonites and a jaw.
Fossils are dug out of rock (for example by hammering it) and stored as evidence of past life.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The **principle of fossil succession**: fossils appear in the rock layers in a definite order, because life changes through time. In a stack of layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest at the top.
**Microfossils** such as **foraminifera** (Cretaceous and Cenozoic) and **conodonts** (Cambrian to Triassic) are very useful index fossils.

boxes.text: Why do shells matter so much? Soft bodies rot or get eaten. Hard shells survive burial, so after 542 Ma the rocks hold many more fossils. Scientists debate whether the Cambrian explosion is real fast evolution, better preservation of hard parts, or a more complete rock record.

Two numbers for the start of life: slide 6 says ~3.8 Ga for life; slide 23 says the first chemical evidence is ~3.5 Ga and the oldest bacterial cell fossils ~3.2 Ga. Match the number to the wording of the question. Textbook 8.4.3 gives 3.5 Ga for the first well-preserved fossils (stromatolites).
Order to remember: single cells (3.8 Ga), oxygen (2 Ga), many cells (700 Ma), shells (542 Ma). Slow, slow, slow, then BOOM.

Tall block diagram of the geologic column listing eons and eras with ages in millions of years, and a key for Ka, Ma and Ga.

img.alt: Spiral diagram of Earth history from the Big Bang to humans, with notes on when life, oxygen, many-celled life and hard shells appeared.

steps.title: Life through geologic time
bullets: **Life first appeared ~3.8 Ga** and early life was **single-celled**. O2 from bacteria built up in the atmosphere by 2 Ga.

Around 700 Ma, multicellular life evolved. Around **542 Ma** the first hard shells appear. Shells make fossils much more likely to survive, and life then diversified rapidly: the **Cambrian explosion**.
Later on the spiral: the age of dinosaurs (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous), then the age of mammals (Cenozoic). The history of life can be laid out against the geologic column.

img.alt: Tall block diagram of the geologic column listing eons and eras with ages in millions of years, and a key for Ka, Ma and Ga.

steps.title: The geologic column
bullets: From oldest to youngest the eons are **Hadean** (back to 4,570 Ma, the birth of the Earth), Archean, Proterozoic, then **Phanerozoic**.
Hadean + Archean + Proterozoic together are the **Precambrian**. The Phanerozoic starts at 542 Ma.
Units: Ka = thousand years, Ma = million years, Ga = billion years.

boxes.text: Why do bones and teeth fossilize best? They are already hard and mineral-rich, so they survive burial. Stronger materials like bone and teeth are the most likely to be preserved, and soft tissue is very rare because bacteria decay it.
Mold = Missing body (a hole). Cast = Copy (the hole filled in, like jelly poured into a jelly mold).

Slides 15-17 and 20 have no captions. Matching each photo to a type here is my reading of the picture (skeleton = bones, shells = shells, ferns = carbonization). Memorize the definitions, not the photos.

Photo of a frozen baby mammoth with its skin and trunk still intact.

steps.title: The eight types
bullets: There are eight types: **frozen or dried body fossils**; body fossils in **amber or tar**; preserved or replaced bones, teeth and shells; permineralized organisms; carbonized impressions; molds and casts; trace fossils; chemical fossils.
**Preserved or replaced hard parts**: bones, teeth and shells, usually with the original material replaced by new minerals that keep the shape. Skeletons and rocks full of shells are typical.
**Carbonization**: tissue is squeezed, volatiles escape, and only a thin film of **carbon** remains. Leaves and ferns are typical.

img.alt: Photo of a frozen baby mammoth with its skin and trunk still intact.

steps.title: Actual preservation
bullets: **Actual preservation** is rare: the original material is kept. A frozen baby mammoth is one example.
Another example is an insect trapped in amber. Mammoth skin and hair also turn up in Arctic deposits.

img.alt: Magnified black-and-white image of tiny, lattice-like microscopic shells with a scale bar of 0.01 mm.

steps.title: Microfossils
bullets: These are tiny, intricate microscopic shells; the scale bar is only 0.01 mm. They are an example of **microfossils**.
Some microfossils, such as foraminifera and conodonts, make very useful index fossils.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Permineralization**: after burial, groundwater minerals fill all the spaces, even inside cells. **Petrified wood** is the example.
**Molds and casts**: the body dissolves and leaves a cavity (the **external mold**). If the cavity is later filled with sediment or mineral, you get a **cast**.

sections.title: Trace and chemical fossils: what organisms DID

boxes.text: Why are trace fossils valuable? One animal can make thousands of footprints but only one skeleton. Footprints also show how it moved, which bones alone cannot.
A burrow or footprint is a trace fossil, NOT a body fossil, even though an animal made it. A coprolite (fossil dropping) is also a trace fossil.

sourceNotes: Slide 22 gives only the three words (observation, analogy, analysis); the explanation of each step is an interpretation.

images.alt: Photo of several footprints pressed into a slab of rock.
Text asking what organisms did that are fossils, with the words observation, analogy and analysis.

img.alt: Photo of several footprints pressed into a slab of rock.

steps.title: Footprints in rock
bullets: **Trace fossils** are indirect evidence: footprints, burrows, droppings (**coprolites**) and stomach stones (gastroliths). This photo shows footprints pressed in rock.
**Ichnology** is the study of tracks. Dinosaur tracks can show size, **gait**, speed and behaviour.
Coprolites and gastroliths give clues about **diet and habitat**.

img.alt: Text asking what organisms did that are fossils, with the words observation, analogy and analysis.

steps.title: Reading a trace
bullets: The question to ask of a trace fossil is: what did the organism **do**? Three steps help: **observation, analogy, analysis**.
One way to read them: observe the trace, compare it (analogy) with what living animals do, then analyze what it means.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Chemical fossils** are chemical signals left behind by life, called **biomarkers** and **isotopes**.

sections.title: How fossils form and why the record is incomplete

boxes.text: Why is burial the key step? Buried bones are protected from scavengers, wind and air. Groundwater and pressure then slowly turn them into rock. A body left on the surface is eaten and scattered.

Slide 39 options: (A) happens every day, (B) is a rare event, (C) does not occur for most organisms, (D) all of the above, (E) is not a result of chance and circumstance. (E) is clearly wrong, since chance and circumstance (for example, quick burial) decide everything. The slide does not print its answer. Textbook 7.3 supports (B) and (C).

images.alt: Block diagrams showing a dinosaur dying, its bones being buried by sediment over time, and later erosion exposing the fossil layer.
Text of a multiple-choice question about how often a life form is preserved as a fossil, from 'happens every day' to 'isn't a result of chance and circumstance'.

img.alt: Block diagrams showing a dinosaur dying, its bones being buried by sediment over time, and later erosion exposing the fossil layer.

steps.title: From death to discovery
bullets: A dinosaur **collapses and dies**. The flesh rots away and the bones remain. Footprints are left in the mud.
The water level rises and **sediment buries** the bones and footprints. A thick sequence of sediments piles up over them and the bones gradually **fossilize**.
Later, **erosion exposes** the layer of strata containing the bones and footprints.

img.alt: Text of a multiple-choice question about how often a life form is preserved as a fossil, from 'happens every day' to 'isn't a result of chance and circumstance'.

steps.title: Why so few become fossils
bullets: Most life today is **soft-bodied or single-celled** and is not likely to be preserved except in unusual conditions.
The **ocean** is the best place for preservation, yet dissolving and scavenging can still destroy remains. On land, burial is even less likely.
So the **fossil record is incomplete**: it records only a small percentage of the life that existed. Preservation as a fossil is a rare event and does not occur for most organisms.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Key idea: fossils need **burial**, then **time**, then luck that erosion brings them to the surface.

Even so, fossils are used for **stratigraphic correlation** (matching same-age layers in different places, using the principle of faunal succession) and to place a formation on the **geologic time scale**.

sections.title: Earliest life: Archean evidence and stromatolites

boxes.text: Why was oxygen 'deadly'? Early life did not use oxygen, so the gas was poison to it. The same waste gas later made breathing animals possible.

Slide says stromatolites ~3.2 Ga; Textbook 8.4.3 says the first well-preserved fossils, stromatolites in Australia, are about 3.5 Ga. Use 3.2 Ga from the slide, and know the textbook value. Also: first chemical evidence (3.5 Ga) is OLDER than the oldest cell fossils (3.2 Ga).

images.alt: Close-up of layered stromatolite rock with a hand on it, and a small inset of microscope images of ancient bacterial cells.
Photo of dark rounded stromatolite domes standing in shallow, clear water.

img.alt: Close-up of layered stromatolite rock with a hand on it, and a small inset of microscope images of ancient bacterial cells.

steps.title: Evidence of the first life
bullets: Life first appeared in the **Archean**, known from **biomarkers and isotopes**. The first chemical evidence of life is ~3.5 Ga.
The **oldest bacterial cell fossils** are ~3.2 Ga (the inset microscope picture has a scale of 10 micrometres).
**Stromatolites** are layered mats of cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) that appeared ~3.2 Ga. The big photo shows layered stromatolite rock.

img.alt: Photo of dark rounded stromatolite domes standing in shallow, clear water.

steps.title: Stromatolites and oxygen
bullets: Stromatolites can look like these dark domes in shallow water.
Cyanobacteria convert **CO2 and H2O** into hydrocarbon food and release a 'catastrophically deadly waste product': **free oxygen**. This changed Earth's atmosphere forever.
O2 had built up in the atmosphere by 2 Ga.

sections.title: Ancient sea animals: ammonoids and the Burgess Shale

boxes.text: Why is a Lagerstatte special? Normally soft bodies are not preserved at all. In rare spots, mud buried animals so well that we can see worms, claws and eyes. That is how we know what Cambrian animals looked like.
Ammonoids and nautiloids are cousins, not the same thing. Nautiloids still live (pearly nautilus); ammonoids are extinct.
Ammonoid = Ancient and gone. Nautilus = Now still here.

sourceNotes: Slide 25 is a video link on ammonoids vs nautiloids; slide 27 (artist's seafloor picture) is unlabelled, so calling it Cambrian is an interpretation.

Photos of rock outcrops beside a stratigraphic column labelled Eldon, Stephen and Cathedral Formations, with a legend of rock types.
Collage of photos of dark, soft-bodied fossil animals preserved on rock.

img.alt: Text announcing a new Burgess Shale site in Kootenay Park, from a 2014 Nature Communications paper.

steps.title: New fossils all the time
bullets: A **new Burgess Shale site** in Kootenay Park was reported in a Nature Communications paper (Feb 11, 2014).
The message: **new fossils are found all the time**.

img.alt: Photos of rock outcrops beside a stratigraphic column labelled Eldon, Stephen and Cathedral Formations, with a legend of rock types.

steps.title: Rock layers at the new site
bullets: This is a **stratigraphic column** (rock layers drawn in order) from the new site: the **Cathedral Formation** at the bottom, the Stephen Formation above it and the Eldon Formation on top.
The legend names the rock types, for example dolostone, shale and carbonate mudstone.

img.alt: Collage of photos of dark, soft-bodied fossil animals preserved on rock.

steps.title: Soft-bodied fossils
bullets: A collage of **soft-bodied fossils** from the new site.
The **Burgess Shale** (found in 1909 by Charles Walcott, western Canada) is a **Lagerstatte**: a site of exceptional preservation including soft body parts.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Ammonoids** are extinct ancient cousins of the pearly **nautilus**, and were the standard index fossil for Triassic correlation.

Common fossil groups: **trilobite, gastropod, bivalve, brachiopod, bryozoan, crinoid, graptolite, ammonite, coral**. Artists' pictures of ancient seafloors show strange animals (one looks like a Cambrian scene).

boxes.text: Why does life look 'perfect'? Nobody designed it. Only individuals whose traits fit the environment leave offspring, so over many generations the population fits its surroundings. Misfits do not pass on their traits.
VARIATION + SURVIVAL + INHERITANCE = natural selection. Like a sieve: the environment is the sieve and traits are the sand.

'Survival of the fittest' means best fit for the environment AND able to reproduce, not simply strongest or biggest. The slide gives only the quote; this meaning comes from the textbook description of natural selection.

images.alt: Text reading 'Theory of evolution: survival of the fittest'.
Text reading 'Evolution happens everyday. Why is life so perfect?'
Text reading 'Theory of evolution: background vs. mass extinction'.

img.alt: Text reading 'Theory of evolution: survival of the fittest'.

steps.title: Survival of the fittest
bullets: The theory of evolution is often summed up as 'survival of the fittest'. Charles Darwin (1809-1882) said life forms evolve into descendant life forms, and **natural selection** is the mechanism.
A **species** is a population with shared characteristics that can reproduce fertile offspring. **Variation** inside a population comes from mixing genes in sexual reproduction and from mutations.
Individuals with a helpful trait survive long enough to reproduce and **pass the trait on**. If too many fail, the species goes **extinct**.

img.alt: Text reading 'Evolution happens everyday. Why is life so perfect?'

steps.title: Evolution happens every day
bullets: Evolution happens every day. Life looks 'so perfect' because natural selection keeps the traits that fit the environment.
If populations become **genetically isolated** (for example on an island), they can become separate species. Evolution is a well-established theory, not just a hypothesis.

img.alt: Text reading 'Theory of evolution: background vs. mass extinction'.

steps.title: Background vs mass extinction
bullets: **Background extinction** is the steady, normal loss of species.
A **mass extinction** is a sudden loss of an unusually large number of species.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The tree of life has three main branches: **Bacteria** and **Archaea** (prokaryotic cells) and **Eukarya** (eukaryotic cells: animals, fungi, plants, ciliates, flagellates, slime molds), all branching from 'proto-life'.

boxes.text: Why does diversity bounce back after each crash? Survivors find empty living space and evolve into new species to fill it. Extinction and evolution work together.

Slide key: T = Tertiary, K = Cretaceous, J = Jurassic, Tr = Triassic, P = Permian, C = Carboniferous, D = Devonian, S = Silurian, O = Ordovician, and the Cambrian symbol on the axis. 'K/T' means Cretaceous/Tertiary, NOT Triassic. The slide gives no percentages, so do not invent any.

images.alt: Line graph of the number of genera through the last 540 million years, with five labelled mass extinction drops.

img.alt: Line graph of the number of genera through the last 540 million years, with five labelled mass extinction drops.

steps.title: Genera through time
bullets: The graph plots **number of genera** (y-axis, up to ~4,000) against **geologic time in millions of years** (x-axis, 500 to 0).
Five **mass extinctions** are labelled: O/T, Late D (Devonian), P/Tr (Permian-Triassic), Tr/J (Triassic-Jurassic) and **K/T** (Cretaceous-Tertiary).
Each mass extinction shows as a sharp drop in the red line, and then the line recovers. Overall the line climbs, and the number of genera is highest today.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The end-Ordovician extinction is the earliest of five mass extinctions in the fossil record. The end of the Paleozoic (Permian) is the **largest** mass extinction in Earth history.

sections.title: DNA as a new tool

boxes.text: Why is DNA useful? Related species share DNA and differences build up over time. Comparing DNA lets scientists draw family trees and estimate when branches split, even for animals like bees that leave few fossils.
DNA is a PARTIAL record. Choose 'partial record', not 'no record' or 'complete record'. (Textbook 7.3.1 mentions only fragments of DNA from rare dinosaur soft tissue.)
For 'why more species now': life keeps spreading into new habitats. Not gravity, the Sun or luck.

sourceNotes: Slides 40-41 do not print their answers; the DNA and 'greater diversity of environments' statements are the only options the sources support. Slide 38's details come from its figure caption.

bullets: **DNA is a new tool** for studying life's past.
A 2013 study (PLoS ONE) gave the first evidence for a **massive extinction event affecting bees** close to the K-T boundary.

img.alt: Circular family tree of four carpenter bee tribes in different colours, with a photo of a bee from each tribe.

steps.title: A carpenter bee family tree
bullets: **Carpenter bees evolved in the Mid Cretaceous**, at the same time as a **dominant type of flowering plants**.
The chart is a **chronogram** (a family tree drawn against time) with four bee tribes: Manueliini, Xylocopini, Ceratinini and Allodapini.

img.alt: Four graphs of computer-simulated lineages in black with a red line for the real bee tree and a blue bar at 65 million years ago.

steps.title: Testing an extinction with models
bullets: Computer simulations of different histories are compared with the real bee tree (the red lines).
The first graph tests a **massive extinction event at 65 Mya** (the caption says 92% of lineages die out). The other three test much lower rates of species birth and death between 90 and 65 Mya.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **DNA carries a partial record** of an organism's evolutionary history.
Many more species exist now because life has become capable of **exploiting a greater diversity of environments**.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of fossilization?
quiz.why: There are eight types: frozen or dried bodies, amber or tar, preserved or replaced hard parts, permineralized organisms, carbonized impressions, molds and casts, trace fossils and chemical fossils. Melting by magma would destroy a body, not fossilize it, so it is not a type.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about fossil ranges and index fossils.
I. A fossil range is the span from a species' first to last appearance.
II. Index fossils are diagnostic of a particular geologic time.
III. Every fossil species has exactly the same range.
quiz.why: I and II are true. III is false because each fossil species has its own unique range.

quiz.q: Why is a widespread, short-lived species a GOOD index fossil?
options: Finding it tells you a narrow slice of time in many places around the world
It is the largest fossil, so it is easy to see
It lived for hundreds of millions of years
It can only be found in one rock layer on Earth
quiz.why: Widespread means you can match layers in many places; short-lived means the match pins down a narrow time interval.

quiz.q: FAD stands for?
quiz.why: FAD is first appearance datum and LAD is last appearance datum.

quiz.q: An insect trapped in amber is best classified as which type of fossilization?
options: a body fossil preserved in amber (actual preservation)
quiz.why: Body fossils preserved in amber or tar are a type of fossilization, and an insect in amber is the classic example of actual preservation.

quiz.q: Why can petrified wood show fine cell detail?
options: The wood is carbonized into a thin film
Groundwater minerals fill all spaces, even cells, after burial (permineralization)
It forms a hollow external mold only
Magma melts and replaces the wood
quiz.why: Permineralization fills every pore, so the cellulose structure is preserved in detail.

quiz.q: A clam shell dissolves, leaving a cavity in the rock. Later, minerals fill the cavity. What is the filled shape called?
quiz.why: The empty cavity is the external mold; once it is filled the result is a cast.

quiz.q: A fern fossil that is a thin black carbon film on rock is an example of?
quiz.why: Carbonization leaves only a carbon silhouette after volatiles are driven out.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about trace fossils.
I. Dinosaur tracks can give information about size, gait and speed.
II. Coprolites can give clues about diet.
III. Burrows are body fossils.
quiz.why: I and II are true (tracks show size, gait and speed; coprolites show diet). Burrows are trace fossils, so III is false.

quiz.q: Why is the fossil record incomplete?
options: Scientists have already found every fossil
Most organisms are soft-bodied or single-celled and burial and preservation are rare
quiz.why: Soft-bodied life is rarely preserved, and even in the ocean dissolving and scavenging limit preservation.

quiz.q: Which describes preservation of a lifeform as a fossil?
options: It happens to nearly every organism
It never depends on chance and circumstance
It is guaranteed if the organism has a brain
It is a rare event that does not happen to most organisms
It occurs only in the Cambrian
quiz.why: Only a small percentage of life is preserved as fossils, so preservation is a rare event that does not happen to most organisms.
quiz.source: Slide 39; Textbook 7.3 (answer not printed on the slide; derived from the textbook)

quiz.q: Which gas did cyanobacteria release that 'changed Earth's atmosphere forever'?
quiz.why: Cyanobacteria convert CO2 and H2O into food and release free oxygen as a deadly waste.

quiz.q: Life first appeared ~3.8 Ga and the first hard shells appeared ~542 Ma. About how long between these, in billions of years?
quiz.why: 3.8 Ga minus 0.542 Ga is about 3.26 Ga, so about 3.3 Ga.

quiz.q: Why did the fossil record get much richer after ~542 Ma?
options: Soft bodies began to fossilize better than shells
Hard shells appeared and increased fossil preservation
quiz.why: Shells increased fossil preservation and life diversified (the Cambrian explosion). Scientists also debate how much of this is real evolution versus better preservation.

quiz.q: In natural selection, why do helpful traits become more common over generations?
options: Individuals with them survive long enough to reproduce and pass them on
The environment changes their DNA to fit
Every individual changes the same amount in one lifetime
quiz.why: Advantaged individuals are more likely to reproduce and pass favored traits to later generations.

quiz.q: On average, how long does a species last in the fossil record?
quiz.why: Around a million years.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a mass extinction labelled on the genera-through-time graph?
quiz.why: The graph labels O/T, Late D, P/Tr, Tr/J and K/T.

quiz.q: What does the overall trend of the genera-through-time graph tell you?
options: Number of genera has steadily fallen to zero
Biodiversity was highest in the Cambrian
Mass extinctions cause drops, but the number of genera recovers and is highest today
The number of genera stays the same through time
quiz.why: The red line drops at each labelled extinction, then rebounds, and ends highest at the present.

quiz.q: Which statement about DNA within lifeforms is correct?
options: It has no record of their evolution
It is found in most fossils
It cannot be used to explore most organisms
It carries a complete record of every ancestor
It carries a partial record of their evolutionary history
quiz.why: DNA is used to study the evolution of groups such as bees. It is a partial record, not a complete one.

quiz.q: Many more species exist now than 3, 2, 1 or 0.5 billion years ago because as life has evolved...
options: it has become capable of exploiting a greater diversity of environments
the Sun has become much brighter
it has become luckier as the universe expanded
it has had time to travel across the planet only
quiz.why: Life spreads into new habitats as it evolves. The other options are not supported by the evidence.
quiz.source: Slide 41 (answer not printed on the slide)

quiz.q: Carpenter bees evolved...
options: in the Mid Cretaceous, at the same time as a dominant type of flowering plants
at the end of the Permian
quiz.why: Carpenter bees evolved in the Mid Cretaceous, at the same time as a dominant type of flowering plants.

quiz.q: Which of these is true of the Burgess Shale?
options: It is a Cambrian site in Australia
It is a site of exceptional preservation including soft body parts
It was discovered in 1990 by Darwin
quiz.why: Charles Walcott found it in 1909 in western Canada; it is a Lagerstatte. A new site was also found in Kootenay Park.

quiz.q: A new layer contains an index fossil whose known range is only the Cretaceous. What can you conclude?
options: The layer is older than every Paleozoic layer
Nothing, index fossils do not help with age
The layer is probably Cretaceous in age
quiz.why: Index fossils are diagnostic of a particular geologic time.

quiz.q: Which step comes FIRST in the fossilization of a dinosaur?
options: The dinosaur dies and flesh rots away, leaving bones
A thick sequence of sediments buries the bones
The water level rises and buries footprints
quiz.why: Death and rotting come first, then burial, then fossilization, then erosion exposes the bed.
